title: Europe's Crazy Spring Heat Wave Breaks 100-Year-Old Records!
summary: Imagine it's only May, but it feels like the hottest day of summer! That's what's happening in Europe right now. The United Kingdom just broke its temperature record for May—twice in two days! On Tuesday, it reached 95.2°F at Kew Gardens in London. The old record was 91.4°F, set way back in 1922. London even had a "tropical night," where the temperature never dropped below 68°F. In France, it hit 97°F. Spain's Seville sizzled at 100°F. That's more than 10 degrees hotter than normal for May. Experts say a "heat dome"—a big bubble of hot air stuck in place—is causing this. And climate change is making these extreme heat waves more likely and more severe. But the heat isn't just uncomfortable—it's dangerous. At least four teenagers drowned in the UK while trying to cool off in lakes. A 60-year-old man died in the sea. In France, at least seven deaths may be linked to the heat, including drownings and people who died during sports. Many homes and schools in the UK don't have air conditioning, so staying cool is really hard. Officials are warning everyone, especially older people, to be careful during the hottest parts of the day. This early heat wave is a scary reminder that our planet is warming up fast.
why_it_matters: When heat waves like this happen, it means you might have more days when it’s too hot to play outside safely, and your school might need better cooling to keep you comfortable.

background_read: Europe’s summers are getting hotter because of climate change. In 2003, a heat wave killed more than 70,000 people across Europe, leading countries to create warning systems.
This May’s heat dome is especially shocking because it happened before summer even started, and some of the broken records were more than 100 years old.

The United Kingdom’s May temperature record, previously set in 1922, was broken twice this week, including at Kew Gardens—a large botanical garden in London that has kept weather records for over a century.
Article_Structure: WHO: People across the United Kingdom, France, and Spain, plus experts and officials.
WHAT: A record‑breaking May heat wave with temperatures above 95°F, driven by a heat dome and climate change, led to deaths from drowning and dehydration.
WHERE: London (Kew Gardens), parts of France, and Seville, Spain.
WHY: The heat dome trapped hot air, and climate change makes these extreme events more frequent and severe; many buildings lack air conditioning, making it harder to stay cool.

perspectives.description: Some people see this as an urgent wake‑up call that might finally push countries to take stronger action against climate change.
The heat wave is dangerous right now—people have died, and many homes without air conditioning are unsafe for the elderly and young children.
Weather experts view this as an important data point to help scientists understand how climate change is speeding up early‑season heat.
